sections.section_title: The First Seal -- The White Horse
sections.summary: The Lamb opens the first seal and a white horse rider is released with a crown given from above, going out conquering, under the authority of the throne room's living creatures and the divine passive 'was given.'

sections.section_title: The Second Seal -- The Red Horse
sections.summary: The second seal releases a red horse whose rider is granted authority to take peace from the earth and cause mutual slaughter, operating under divine permission signaled by the repeated divine passive.

sections.section_title: The Third Seal -- The Black Horse
sections.summary: The third seal releases a black horse whose rider carries scales, representing severe but measured famine with inflated grain prices while oil and wine are preserved, reflecting proportional and restrained divine judgment drawn from the covenant-curse tradition.

sections.section_title: The Fourth Seal -- The Pale Horse
sections.summary: The fourth seal releases Death and Hades, given authority over a fourth of the earth to kill by sword, famine, pestilence, and wild beasts, replicating Ezekiel's four judgments within explicitly limited scope.

sections.section_title: The Fifth Seal -- The Souls Under the Altar
sections.summary: The fifth seal reveals the souls of those slain for the word of God and their maintained testimony, located under the heavenly altar as sacrificial offerings, crying 'How long?' and told to rest until the number of their fellow servants yet to be killed is completed.
sections.relevance: The martyrs are under the altar 'because of the testimony which they had maintained' -- their faithfulness is presented as their own sustained action, not as a status imposed upon them. The verb 'maintained' (eichon) frames their testimony-keeping as genuine human commitment with lethal consequences they accepted. The predetermined 'number to be completed' concerns the timing of God's final vindication, not the predetermination of who will be faithful. The neutral reading's conclusion that 'the outcome is determined by present faithfulness, not by past status or external identity' places this passage within a framework where human agency in maintaining testimony determines one's standing before God.
key_phrases: because of the testimony which they had maintained
the number of their fellow servants and their brethren who were to be killed even as they had been, would be completed
there was given to each of them a white robe

sections.section_title: The Sixth Seal -- Cosmic Upheaval and the Wrath of the Lamb
sections.summary: The sixth seal brings cosmic upheaval -- earthquake, darkened sun, blood-red moon, falling stars, rolled-up sky, displaced mountains -- causing all categories of humanity to hide and cry for the mountains to fall on them rather than face the wrath of the Lamb, culminating in the question 'who is able to stand?'
sections.relevance: The question 'who is able to stand?' frames survival of the day of wrath as contingent rather than predetermined. The neutral reading connects this directly to the conditional promises of chapters 2-3: 'the answer, as chapters 2-3 made clear, depends on their present faithfulness: whether they conquer, whether they hold fast, whether they do not deny the name.' The standing is described as 'not automatic or guaranteed to all; it belongs to those whose faithfulness has prepared them for this day.' The seven-category list of terrified humanity (kings through slaves) emphasizes that no social status provides exemption, but the document's own answer in chapter 7 identifies those who can stand as those who 'washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb' -- an action attributed to the individuals themselves. The ability to endure eschatological judgment is presented as the outcome of sustained human faithfulness, not of prior divine selection.
key_phrases: every slave and free person hid themselves
the great day of their wrath has come
